name: Zinc-based deodorant (Zinc ricinoleate)

lead: Zinc ricinoleate is an ingredient in many deodorants that is said to adsorb odor, capturing odor molecules rather than masking them, which appeals to people avoiding aluminium.

It is the zinc salt of ricinoleic acid, a main fatty acid in castor oil. Wikipedia describes the mechanism as unclear, and a 2000 simulation study examined the adsorption. No clinical studies of zinc ricinoleate deodorants were found.

paras: Found in stick and spray deodorants and used as an everyday underarm product, often chosen as an alternative to antiperspirants. It does not stop sweat.
Safety information was not found in the reviewed sources.

angle.text: Zinc ricinoleate, a castor-oil zinc salt, is added to deodorants to capture odor molecules, and is mentioned as an alternative to aluminium antiperspirants. Its mechanism is described as unclear, and no clinical studies were found.

lead: Zinc ricinoleate is the zinc salt of ricinoleic acid, a main fatty acid in castor oil.[1] Many deodorants include it as an odor-adsorbing ingredient, meaning it is said to capture odor molecules rather than mask them or stop sweat.[1] In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions it is mentioned as an alternative to aluminum antiperspirants.
Wikipedia states that the mechanism of this activity is unclear.[1] No clinical studies of zinc ricinoleate deodorants were found.

paras: Zinc ricinoleate is found in many deodorants as an adsorber of odor.[1] Deodorants generally work by masking odor or preventing it, unlike antiperspirants that reduce sweating, typically through aluminium salts plugging sweat ducts.[2] Early deodorants used zinc oxide among other ingredients.[2]
Proponents say it neutralizes odor molecules without blocking sweat. Wikipedia describes the mechanism as unclear and cites a 2000 molecular dynamics simulation study of its odor adsorption.[1]
The sources reviewed contain no safety or toxicity information for the compound specifically.
